content.p: The Red Devils Motorcycle Club is, according to police and analysts, a club through which the Hells Angels bring in and test new men. Police and analysts in several countries describe it as the Angels' official support club, one whose members do work for the senior gang and hope to be promoted into it. Its name is easy to confuse with an older Canadian club that carried the same words, but La Presse stressed that they are not the same group.

Because the club sits beneath a far better known organisation, much of what is public about it comes from police briefings and from court filings. Those are accusations, not findings. The most serious of them, a 2024 federal indictment in North Carolina, charges five alleged members with a murder; the defendants have not been convicted of it and the lawyer for one said that everyone is innocent until proven guilty.

Nova Scotia's criminal intelligence service gave a plain description in 2021. Det. Const. Jeff Tremblett said support clubs are small groups aligned with a larger, more powerful gang. They copy its structure, follow its orders, help with criminal activity, shield the dominant club from prosecution, and serve as a recruiting ground. They also send money upward by selling shirts and hats carrying the senior gang's logos. He added that most motorcycle clubs are made up of law-abiding people and that only about one per cent are outlaw gangs.

Global News interviewed François Doré, formerly of the Sûreté du Québec, in 2023. He said young men join the Red Devils to work their way toward becoming full Hells Angels. In his words, they do drug dealing and money laundering for the senior team, and the violence and illegal activity is meant to prove they are safe and not talking to police. An Ontario Provincial Police sergeant quoted by Vice in 2015 put the recruitment logic in similar terms: the Angels recruit from the Red Devils because they know those men are loyal, are not informants and are not police officers.

Prosecutors in North Carolina described the ladder in an indictment reported in 2024. Men entered as "hangarounds", became "prospects" sponsored by members, and earned a full patch as Hells Angels. The Red Devils, the indictment said, acted as both recruiters and potential Hells Angels.
content.h2: Origins and the confusion over the name
content.p: La Presse reported in 2014 that the Red Devils were created in 2001, when two groups of bikers, from northern Massachusetts and from Karlstad, Sweden, were invited to adopt the colours. On its website the club billed itself as the sole official support group of the Hells Angels anywhere in the world, in La Presse's French rendering. Like the Angels' 81, it uses a number as a symbol, 184. La Presse put its size at more than 130 chapters, many of them in Germany, according to the club's own website. Seven News had reported two years earlier that the website claimed about 120 chapters worldwide.

The name already existed in Canada. The original Red Devils, a club from Hamilton, Sudbury and Chatham in Ontario, had been riding for roughly 66 years. In 2015 Vice reported that all 31 of its members patched over to Bacchus MC, a decision their former leader Ray Philp said was influenced by the arrival of the new Red Devils. Philp recalled that in 2002 he had met US leaders of the new club who assured him they would not enter Canada out of respect for his. Journalist Peter Edwards described the original club as blue-collar riders who were not troublemakers. La Presse noted that Walter Stadnick, a former Hells Angels national president, had once been in the Hamilton club, but that it was not the same group as today's Red Devils.

La Presse reported in July 2014 that a Red Devils section had appeared in Montreal, after the Hells Angels had reopened their Montreal chapter in May. Operation SharQc, a police sweep in April 2009, had gutted the Angels in Quebec. A source told the newspaper that the Red Devils had just been given hierarchical power over the other support groups in the province. Vice quoted La Presse reporter Daniel Renaud as saying that in the nineties the Angels in Canada had relied on support clubs such as the Rockers, Death Riders and Jokers. Vice counted chapters in Montreal, Barrie, Toronto, Ottawa and two on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River within a year.

In Atlantic Canada, a criminologist at Saint Mary's University, Stephen Schneider, told the Canadian Press in 2018 that the Red Devils were roughly the Angels' "AAA affiliate" and that their arrival showed the Angels were serious about the region. The Halifax chapter, set up that July, was recruited from the Gate Keepers and the Darksiders, according to RCMP Staff Sgt. Guylaine Cottreau. The Red Devils also had a chapter in Moncton, and in January 2023 a clubhouse with Red Devils signage opened on the main street of Shediac, New Brunswick. The RCMP there said it received no calls for service over the weekend a gathering of outlaw club members took place.
CBC gave two dates for the end of the Angels' only Nova Scotia chapter: 1999 in its 2019 report and 2001 in its 2021 report.

In April 2020 the RCMP in New Brunswick announced that four men had been arrested between 17 February and 9 April in an investigation into organised crime, drugs and money laundering. They were a 34-year-old prospect and a 29-year-old full-patch member of the Red Devils, and two Hells Angels, a prospect and a full-patch member of its Nomads chapter. All were released pending court appearances. Inspector Ron Desilva said the Red Devils operate under the Angels' direction.

In 2024 Ontario Provincial Police searched the Hells Angels and Red Devils clubhouses in Hamilton after a July bar robbery. Four Hells Angels members and one Red Devils member were among five men charged with assault causing bodily harm and robbery, and police said they seized firearms and body armour. Global News, reporting on another OPP raid in the Waterloo Region, noted that a house outside Peterborough had previously displayed "Red Devils MC Peterborough" insignia before switching to Hells Angels signs in May 2024.

In September 2010 Larry "Ronnie" Capps Jr., president of the club's Cape Fear chapter, was arrested in Brunswick County, North Carolina, after searches that turned up 50 firearms, more than $3,000 and an ounce of cocaine. The sheriff released video he said showed Capps selling half an ounce of cocaine to an undercover officer, one of eleven recorded transactions. Capps's bond was raised to $1.2 million after the court found threats against investigators' families credible. The sheriff said the arrest had nothing to do with any motorcycle club.
The Boston Globe recalled that in March 2013 raids on hangouts in Lynn and Byfield, Massachusetts, led to arrests of several Hells Angels and Red Devils on kidnapping, mayhem and extortion charges.

On 19 March 2022, an assault at a gas station in Fayetteville, North Carolina, was followed that night by a shooting at the Baymont Ramada hotel on Owen Drive. Investigators said four clubs were involved: the Hells Angels, Red Devils, Infamous Ryders and La Familia. William Franklin Davis Sr., 42, died at the scene, and Keith Allan Dickey, 37, and Donald Dillenbeck, 49, died in hospital; three others were wounded. Two men were charged over the earlier assault, Dalton Emmanuel Laperriere and Kerry Helms Lawing, each with assault with a deadly weapon inflicting serious injury and felony conspiracy. Reports quoted here do not say who fired the shots.

On 1 January 2023, Jonas Padilla, a member of the Pagans Motorcycle Club, was killed in north Raleigh after falling from his motorcycle. People living nearby reported hearing gunshots and seeing bikes speed away. CBS 17 spells his surname Padia; ABC11, WRAL and the AOL report give Padilla.

Warrants described by WRAL said surveillance video showed Padilla being chased by five motorcyclists and falling down an embankment, after which two people in helmets removed his club vest. The five riders were wearing Red Devils vests, the warrants said. Five men, accused of being Red Devils, were charged with murder within days and held on state charges.

In October 2024 federal prosecutors announced a sixteen-defendant, eight-count indictment in what they called an operation against the Hells Angels and Red Devils, the first racketeering case in North Carolina since a 2017 case against Bloods members. The five men, Vidaul Rashaad Reed, Anthony Edward Cheever, David William Stephens, Martinus Jermaine Starks and Tyler Scott Grissom, were charged with murder in aid of racketeering and discharging a firearm causing death. A conviction on the murder count carries a mandatory life sentence. Two others, one a Red Devils member and one a Hells Angel, were charged as accessories after the fact. Eight Hells Angels were charged with attempted murder and assault in aid of racketeering over an attack on Pagans in a Dairy Queen parking lot in Wade in July 2023, and one man was charged with witness tampering.

U.S. Attorney Michael Easley said the Angels and Red Devils had a "standing green light" to attack Pagans. An attorney for one murder defendant said everyone is innocent until proven guilty. No verdict had been reported in the coverage found.

Seven News reported in 2012 that the Red Devils had set up a chapter in the Logan region of Queensland, with about 11 members in Brisbane, and that police were "very, very closely monitoring" it. In November 2013 Daniel Pegoraro, 28, a patched Red Devils member in Melbourne, survived two gunshots to the back outside his parents' home in Epping. SBS reported that police had not yet linked it to the Hells Angels' feud with the Bandidos and that he was refusing to cooperate. The report also said he had been named in court as a suspect in a failed attack on a Bandidos enforcer but never charged.

In 2025 a Victorian newspaper reported that the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission lists the Red Devils among 35 outlaw motorcycle gangs, and that the state's new insignia offence, which came into force on 25 August, applies only to organisations named in regulations.
